# Component Structure Scope Decision Record

This record preserves the choice made when the component generation requirements for 6.0-beta.1 were finalized. The dispute was not about whether to continue having a component blueprint, but about exactly what the term "component structure" covered. The requirement name included both flat and nested. If the scope were written as supporting only flat, nested would be excluded before implementation began; if only a broad statement such as "support component structures" remained, it would provide no basis later for deciding whether a generated result belonged to this round of work.

The decision remains: the component structure scope for 6.0-beta.1 is limited to flat and nested. This sentence defines a requirement boundary, not a directory design or a description of the current generator's internal organization. It allows regression testing to establish observations around the two explicitly named structures, while avoiding treating forms that were never discussed as existing commitments.

## Initial Trade-offs

The initial draft compared not multiple implementations, but three ways of defining the requirements.

| Definition | Decision | Reason at the time |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Retain only flat | Not adopted | nested already appeared among the requirement targets, and removing it would narrow the scope to be addressed. |
| Include flat and nested side by side | Adopted | Both structures have an explicit place, and regression testing can verify their generated results separately. |
| Leave the structures unspecified for now | Not adopted | Without a defined structure scope, there is no shared standard for any claim that something is "supported." |

The third definition looks conservative, but in practice it would defer the judgment. One person could consider the work complete based on a local implementation, while another could consider it not yet started based on structures that were not covered; neither would have the same scope baseline. Choosing flat and nested was not intended to claim that their implementations were identical, but to first give the component generation work a boundary against which it could be assessed.

Retaining only flat was equally unacceptable. It would turn nested, which had already been explicitly named, into an exception rather than part of the scope. Once that exception was left out of the decision, it would be easy for later regression additions to include only flat samples and then treat nested as a future additional request. That narrowing approach was not adopted here.

## What the Decision Covers

This decision covers the types of structures that can be discussed under this round of component generation requirements. It requires subsequent records to treat flat and nested as two targets that must be reflected in user-visible results, rather than treating "structure" as a catch-all term that can be extended at will.

It does not prescribe a fixed directory for flat or a fixed file tree for nested. The current material provides no such output samples, so complete paths, filenames, or template forms cannot be inferred from the two names. If mappings, tokens, or branches exist in the implementation, those are local facts that must be verified individually during review, and should not be written back into the requirements themselves.

It also does not prescribe uniform handling for unlisted structures. Unlisted structures receive no support commitment from this record, but there is also insufficient material here to classify all of them as rejected, ignored, or compatible. That is a separate compatibility judgment requiring concrete inputs and results. Writing "all other inputs will fail" in place of "not included in this scope" would make a stronger claim than the decision made at the time.

Likewise, the decision does not treat the generator's internal helper function names as stable interfaces. Internal names may change as the implementation is split, merged, or renamed; a name remaining in place does not prove that a nested result exists, and a name changing does not mean that a flat result is no longer valid. The scope choice should withstand changes in internal organization without depending on the continued existence of a particular helper function.

## Boundaries Left by the Initial Draft

The initial draft stated only that the two structures were retained, and noted that unlisted structures were not implicit targets. At the time, this was enough to reject the approach of "leaving the structures unspecified for now," but not enough to answer two implementation-side questions: what flat ultimately generates, and what nested ultimately generates.

This gap did not change the initial decision. The scope decision first answers which targets must be included in the work; output review then answers what each target actually leaves in the repository. When the two are mixed together, a piece of code along a path can easily be misread as product scope, or conversely, requirement terms can be treated as already verified output. v1 did not connect these two layers, so its brief conclusion should simply be retained, without retroactively inserting the later review status into it.

The initial draft also had no related cards to cite. At that point, only `blueprints/component/index.js` was retained as a starting point for looking back, as a reminder to check the actual references at that revision later. This starting point was recorded because earlier investigation notes already pointed here through terms such as blueprint, generation, component, flat, nested, and componentstructure; it was not a conclusion about all call relationships.

## The Role of the File Entry Point

Subsequent review still starts from `blueprints/component/index.js`, using `v_prev` of `internal/ember-runtime` as the reference. This file is suitable for examining local declarations of the component blueprint, structure options, and nearby generation handling. It provides a repeatable starting point and keeps "structure scope" and "implementation location" from becoming completely disconnected.

However, a file entry point answers where to begin checking, not which file inherently owns the entire requirement. Structure options may appear here while the generated results are formed through other references; a nearby token may also be unrelated to this scope. During review, first confirm whether flat and nested are still identifiable options near the entry point, then follow the actual references at the time to see how they affect the generated results. References that have not been traced through cannot be filled in based on directory location.

This distinction has practical implications for later maintenance. If a structure option is found to have moved elsewhere, the implementation record should be supplemented or the verification entry point adjusted, rather than removing flat and nested from the scope decision. Conversely, if a piece of code remains in this file but has no corresponding user-visible result, regression coverage cannot be declared solely because it is near the entry point.

Terms such as classic, pod, filemaptokens, or structure appearing near the path do not automatically expand the decision on this page either. They are navigation terms available from the earlier investigation, not new structure commitments. Including all of them in the scope would mix local implementation vocabulary and requirement targets into the same layer, making it difficult later to determine exactly which change triggered a regression.

## Regression Addendum

EMR-216 later described the to-do item as: add a repository regression test for "Limit component structures to flat and nested," asserting user-visible results rather than internal helper function names. In the recorded activity, the card moved from To Do to In Progress on 2025-10-06. This action shows that regression work had begun, not that the tests had passed, and it provided no snapshots, file lists, or fixed outputs that could be copied directly into this page.

Regression testing should let readers distinguish whether flat and nested have each been handled. Merely proving that the blueprint entry point was executed is not enough to prove that the requested structure appears in the generated artifacts; merely proving that a token was replaced is also not enough to prove that the result users see matches the scope. Checkpoints should focus on observable results after generation, rather than treating internal calls as the sole criterion.

"Verify separately" here does not mean requiring both structures to share one set of directory assertions. The current record provides no basis for requiring them to generate the same files, paths, or content. A reasonable regression test can retain a minimal visible observation for each structure, as long as that observation shows that the request was not swallowed during generation and does not lock internal implementation details into external behavior.

If future tests cover only flat, even consistent passes would show only that observations for flat have been established; they cannot stand in for nested. If tests check only a shared helper function, a successful function call still cannot tell us whether the two requests produce different or complete results. If tests cover both requests but assert only against intermediate objects, an additional layer of post-generation observation is still needed. These three gaps are different in nature and should not be closed with the blanket statement that "component tests already exist."

The current material also provides no failure samples. This page therefore does not invent expected filenames, directory levels, text content, or error behavior for flat or nested. When adding records of actual tests, retain the revision used together with the generated results; writing only "tested" would prevent later readers from determining whether the checks concerned the scope, internal calls, or some output that happened to still exist.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Scope_pending
    Scope_pending --> Retain_flat_and_nested
    Retain_flat_and_nested --> Regression_pending
    Regression_pending --> Regression_in_progress
    Regression_in_progress --> User_results_pending_confirmation
```

"Regression in progress" in the diagram corresponds only to the state in which work on EMR-216 had begun. It does not mean that user results have been confirmed, much less that a new third structure has been accepted. The scope decision already existed before regression work began; the task of subsequent checks is to connect the decision to repository behavior, not to decide again whether flat and nested belong to this round of work.

## Ways of Writing That Can Overstep the Scope

Describing flat and nested as two fixed directories is the first way to go beyond the available material. A file structure may be an implementation result, but the decision retained only structure types, not a directory contract. Unless subsequent regression testing provides actual output, directory guesses cannot be turned into rules.

Treating the entry-point file as the sole home of the implementation is another way. `blueprints/component/index.js` is the starting point for review, not shorthand for all paths. If actual references point elsewhere, they should be added to the implementation-side record; this page only needs to maintain the relationship between the scope choice and the verification starting point.

Another misreading is to mix adjacent work into this item. DOC-23 records an interface review of legacy component-test blueprint hooks. Like this page, it is part of the work around beta.1, so it can serve as a neighboring document for navigation, but whether the hooks stay or go is not a prerequisite for flat or nested, nor can the generated results of component structures be inferred from it.

Finally, "there is no commitment for unlisted structures" must not be rewritten as "new structures will never be allowed in the future." If later requirements propose a third structure, its relationship to flat and nested should be assessed separately: is it additional scope, a replacement for one of them, or only an internal implementation detail. A new target can be included in the same set of regression criteria only by explicitly changing this decision.

## Results Still to Be Added

What needs to be added now is concrete review results, not a reinterpretation of the reasons for the choice:

- The user-visible generated results of a flat request, and the corresponding regression coverage location;
- The user-visible generated results of a nested request, and the corresponding regression coverage location;
- The confirmed reference nodes in `v_prev` between `blueprints/component/index.js` and the generated results;
- Test output, once regression work is complete, showing that the two structures were each observed.

Once these items are complete, the scope, entry point, and actual results can be connected into a reviewable record. Until they are complete, there is still only one currently valid conclusion: the component structure work for 6.0-beta.1 is bounded by flat and nested, without also deciding directory layout, internal function naming, or compatibility behavior for other structures.

# Proposal for adjusting legacy hooks in component tests

This proposal records an attempt to narrow the scope of the component-test blueprint. The target was still `blueprints/component-test/qunit-rfc-232-files/__root__/__testType__/__path__/__test__.ts`; the earlier investigation followed the names component-test, blueprint, and hooks back to this template. The first draft called it the "entry point for legacy hooks," but that description was never refined into a more precise location.

The three declarations at the start of the template were the only adjacent items explicitly recorded at the time:

```ts
import { setupRenderingTest } from '<%= modulePrefix %>/tests/helpers';
import { render } from '@ember/test-helpers';
import { setupTest } from '<%= modulePrefix %>/tests/helpers';
```

The risk in the first draft was treating them as the same kind of legacy artifact because they appeared together. Their names and origins differ, and `__testType__` in the template also affects which type of test is ultimately generated. Even if the removal target is indeed the legacy component-test hooks, that is not a reason to mark all three imports for deletion. Doing so would replace "stop generating the legacy hook" with "generated files no longer need test setup or rendering calls."

## The two options at the time

The conservative option was to leave the template unchanged and first collect component-test still generated by the blueprint. That would leave existing output unchanged, but newly generated tests would continue to include the legacy hooks, only postponing the problem.

The other option was to first remove the clearly identifiable snippets that generate legacy hooks, leaving the rest of the template structure untouched. This option had a smaller migration scope: callers would not be required to rewrite existing tests as part of this change. The trade-off was that it could only establish that this generation branch no longer produced that snippet, not that the entire component-test system was free of legacy hooks.

The proposal leaned toward the second option at the time, but the condition was not "delete any import you see." First map the hook's specific injection point to the branches of `__testType__`; if the snippet exists only in one type of generated test, limit the change to that type. Whether to keep `setupRenderingTest`, `render`, and `setupTest` should depend on what is still actually written into the generated tests, not on whether their names appear near component-test.

## Review addendum

EMR-218 was later submitted for review, with a note stating that implementation had been completed on an existing branch. This changed the purpose of this page: it was no longer waiting for a decision on whether to start a trial implementation, but checking whether the proposal had overstated the implementation's scope. The card still retained an unfinished verification task: find a caller still using "Remove legacy component-test blueprint hooks" and check the actual version, entry point, and current result.

The smallest acceptable change at review was still to handle only template output that could be identified as a legacy hook, retaining test helper declarations that were not used exclusively by that output. If an actual generation entry point shows that the legacy hook is still needed after deletion, restore the corresponding template snippet first, then record that entry point and the test type it uses separately. Do not hide a change in generated output by renaming callers, adding a compatibility layer, or deleting unrelated imports.

Earlier, someone interpreted "remove the hook" as stripping the component-test template down to ordinary test structure. That view is retained here to explain why `setupTest` was also brought into the discussion at the time; it is not a confirmed implementation direction. Instead, the available material supports only a narrower proposal: if legacy hooks have an identifiable generation point, remove them from that point; retain the template's other direct dependencies individually or investigate them separately.

Two points remain unconfirmed: whether different `__testType__` share the same hook snippet, and whether the caller found actually covers rendering tests. EMR-218 can serve as a starting point for further investigation; this page does not supply a passing or failing run record for it.

# Glimmer Lifecycle Migration Procedure

This migration starts with a legacy call in the help page. The caller reads component lifecycle state according to the page instructions, and `packages/@ember/-internals/glimmer/lib/glimmer-component-docs.ts` was the verification point available at the time. This path is suitable for confirming the name "lifecycle state" and the surrounding description; it cannot replace confirmation of the actual implementation location.

The initial handling classified the symptom as a documentation gap between the help page and the component instance: the legacy call appeared to be missing a prerequisite that should have been stated. On review, that classification was insufficient. The legacy call fails in directories without preinitialized state, so the issue is not limited to the page text and call parameters. During migration, "the call happens too early" must be considered separately from "the state itself was not provided"; either situation can make the caller appear to work in existing directories.

```text
Legacy help-page call
    |
    +-- Directory with preinitialized state: previously used as the primary verification scenario

Migration verification
    |
    +-- Directory without preinitialized state
    +-- Lifecycle phase in which the state is read
    +-- Move the caller only after confirming the implementation location
```

## Record the Call Site First

When locating the legacy call from the help page, record which state the call site depends on rather than recording only the component name. Then note whether it is near component creation, normal rendering, or destruction. The same term appearing in different phases does not mean the state is equally readable. In particular, do not replace a destruction-adjacent call just because the normal rendering path passes.

After opening `packages/@ember/-internals/glimmer/lib/glimmer-component-docs.ts`, do only two things: verify whether the lifecycle state described by the help page is still the object assumed at the call site; and check whether the navigation near the description can lead to the implementation area that needs confirmation. Do not put post-migration behavior here, and do not treat the documentation file as the location where the state is initialized. If the documentation and implementation point to different places, stop at this call site instead of expanding based on name similarity.

## Migration Batches

1. First select one legacy call as a sample and verify it in a directory without preinitialized state. That directory is the boundary for this verification; it must not be replaced with an environment where the caller's state has already been prepared.
2. If the sample fails, preserve the phase and call site where the failure occurred. Do not write the state during directory initialization first; that would turn the state-source problem into a prerequisite that only appears to pass.
3. After confirming the implementation location, move the same class of call sites. Handle only one read timing per batch, then review destruction-adjacent calls separately at the end of the batch.
4. Normal rendering after migration can be a local result, but it cannot vouch for the destruction phase. Whether a component being destroyed can read the same state must continue to be confirmed at each call site.

EMR-224 record the legacy call's failure in a directory without preinitialized state. The card was later confirmed by its owner, then had its owner changed after the issue was traced to another part of the implementation. This change affects the migration order: before continuing, use the implementation location currently referenced by the card rather than following the route that initially assigned the issue to the documentation layer based on the help page.

## Restore the Legacy Path

If a caller fails in a scenario without preinitialized state after being changed, first restore that caller to its pre-change form, then compare the triggering conditions before and after restoration. Restoration is used to determine whether the failure was introduced by this migration; it does not mean the legacy path can continue as a compatibility solution. The legacy call is the object being verified, and passing cannot be obtained by writing the state in advance.

If the failure appears only near destruction, stop the remaining replacements in this batch. Record both the phase of the call site and why it still needs to read the state, and wait for the current implementation location to be confirmed. At this point, do not force the destruction call to use the normal-rendering read pattern, and do not close the issue because it cannot be reproduced in existing directories.

This page covers only the migration, batch verification, and restoration actions for legacy calls to Glimmer component lifecycle state. Standalone rendering results and the matter of publishing standalone rendering through `@ember/renderer` are recorded by DOC-26; do not combine the two paths into the same compatibility replacement.

# Standalone rendering: callable contract

Revision quality-repair-010-20260920-r1; applies to EMR-226 and EMR-227.

`renderComponent(component, options)` takes two positional arguments. The first is a component definition with an associated template, not the target element. The second is an object with these exact fields:

- `into` (required): the target DOM/SimpleDOM element, or a cursor `{ element, nextSibling }`, with `nextSibling` null or a node in that element.
- `owner` (optional): an object, defaulting to a new empty object. Service/helper lookup needs the corresponding Owner methods. An explicit owner may be shared across renders.
- `args` (optional): a named-argument object, default `{}`. Properties are passed as `@name`; reactive getters remain reactive rather than being snapshotted once.
- `env` (optional): renderer settings. `isInteractive` defaults to true (false disables modifiers); `document` defaults to `globalThis.document`; `hasDOM` defaults to true. Non-browser callers supply a compatible document and appropriate `hasDOM`/`isInteractive` values. Other renderer settings are private pass-through, not additional public requirements.

The synchronous return is an object with `destroy(): void`. No other result members are required. Initial content is rendered before return; reactive updates and teardown settle through the Ember run loop. `run(() => result.destroy())` clears that render, is safe to repeat, and does not destroy a caller-supplied owner or its other renders. Destroying the owner through `@glimmer/destroyable` clears its associated renders even when results were discarded. See DOC-27's current revision for direction and ownership.

`@ember/renderer` exports the same `renderComponent` function identity as the internal renderer export, not a wrapper. A minimal call is `renderComponent(Definition, { into: element })` when a global document is available; a headless call supplies `env: { document, hasDOM: false, isInteractive: false }`. Optional fields may be omitted independently.

This revision specifies valid inputs. It does not prescribe new validation/error strings for malformed options, missing component definitions, or unavailable DOM globals; do not invent a hidden error-text contract for those inputs. Compiler/resolver error contracts elsewhere remain unchanged.

# Standalone Rendering Teardown Decision Record — Direction Correction

Revision quality-repair-010-20260920-r1; current acceptance criteria for EMR-228.

Versions 1 and 2 are retained historical drafts, not the current ownership contract. The Result --> Owner arrow in version 2 reverses the association direction; it cannot override the owner-driven-render-cleanup in the instruction.

The current upstream target is "Tear down standalone rendering with its owner". The owner manages the associated render result: after the owner is destroyed, the target element must be cleared even if the caller never retained or invoked result.destroy. The caller remains responsible for the lifecycle of its external owner. result.destroy only destroys that render; it cannot destroy the shared owner in turn or clear other standalone renderings under the same owner. Destroying the result first and then the owner, as well as repeating result.destroy, should all be safe. Observe the cleanup results after the run loop converges.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    OwnerDestroy[destroy owner] --> RenderA[clear associated render A]
    OwnerDestroy --> RenderB[clear associated render B]
    ResultDestroy[result A destroy] --> RenderA
    ResultDestroy -. does not destroy .-> OwnerAlive[owner and render B remain live]
```

Nested rendering reactivity and the destroying guard are still accepted against EMR-230; this correction does not reduce that scope. The public call shape is in the current version of DOC-26; look up core-05 to continue verifying standalone rendering, shared owners, and cleanup boundaries. # Caller Integration Two-State Anomaly Postmortem

The integration session left two records pointing to the same object, but the two records showed different states. The first item compared was resolver registration; it did not match the old record. At the time, there was no reliable timestamp, so it was impossible to tell whether this was a state transition in the object, a lag in the record, or two inputs being viewed together.

No further retries were made during the session. Further attempts would produce subsequent results, while the anomaly itself was that the same object appeared in different states across different records. The original input and entry-point version were saved first at `docs/adj-ember/incidents/ember-client-integration-two-states-for-one-object.md`. This step only preserved the difference seen at the time; it did not reconstruct the full request context.

At the time, two things could be confirmed separately:

- After owner destruction, the path that had been stuck could recover;
- Why consumer regression changed was still unknown.

The former was an observation made during recovery; the latter required the original input to continue the replay. The fact that recovery occurred does not make owner destruction a prescribed fix; nor does the consumer-side change appearing alongside it establish a causal link between them.

The old screenshot only shows that someone had seen a state difference at the time. It does not contain enough request information to explain on its own why the other path was working normally, much less serve as a substitute for the entry-point version. Someone at the session treated the resolver registration difference as the cause; that was the initial working hypothesis, not a confirmed attribution.

One blank was left on the page at the time:

```text
Missing timestamp: ____
```

The blank was not filled in with an exact time. On a later review, first open the preserved original record and distinguish the initial state, the path that later recovered, and the still-unconfirmed consumer regression. Do not fill in unrecorded actions as speculation, or backfill the post-recovery result as a cause confirmed at the outset.

# Review of the Two-State Anomaly in Caller Integration

This record originally only noted "the same object appeared in two states" and that resolver registration differed from the old record. On later review, the issue was not simply whether there was a path that ultimately recovered, but that the two records had no common reference point in time. The current revision seen at the two time points was different, so the before-and-after states and trends cannot be directly subtracted.

The initial page placed the discrepancy, the save action, and the later recovery next to one another, making it easy to read them as one continuous validation. What was actually preserved was a very narrow slice of the incident: when a call sample involving @ember passed through the adapter boundary, the record showed a state discrepancy; the original input and entry version were saved afterward; only later did we see a user path recover. No material connects these three events into a single cause.

## Order of the Incident Evidence

| Relative time | What was left behind | Action taken at the time |
|---|---|---|
| T+00 | `ember-caller-integration-same-object-appears-in-two-states` deviated from the original record | Save the original input and entry version |
| T+07 | `Rollup input graph` was still normal | Do not expand the scope to all call samples |
| T+18 | The comparison pointed to `workspace package entrypoint` | Leave that branch for further review through the corresponding maintenance entry |
| T+31 | User path recovered | Root cause remained unconfirmed |

T+00 to T+31 only indicate the order in which the incident records were arranged; they are not times that can be joined to absolute clocks on other pages. The old version lacked complete time points, so the table merely places the existing fragments back in relative position; it does not mean that every item came from the same request context.

The earliest wording was "resolver registration differed from the old record." It remains here because it did trigger the decision to stop further retries and preserve the incident evidence. It does not mean that "resolver registration is the root cause": at the time, only one visible discrepancy had been seen; there was no material showing what the object went through before and after the discrepancy, and no material ruling out the influence of the entry version or recording time.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Call sample
    participant I as @ember integration
    participant R as Incident record
    participant W as On-duty handling
    C->>I: Use the original input
    I->>R: Record a state discrepancy
    R-->>W: Different resolver registration
    W-->>R: Save the version, do not continue retrying
    W-->>C: Path recovered, cause under investigation
```

The diagram only retains the short path being handled at the time. It does not mean that all call samples passed through it in this order, nor that the final hop had confirmed the root cause. In particular, the recovery at T+31 only shows that the user path recovered at that stage; it cannot be expanded to mean that all entry points, all callers, or all revisions were already consistent.

## Limits of the Two Comparisons

`Rollup input graph` was still normal at T+07, which once caused the investigation scope to narrow quickly. This result only shows that the view at that point did not immediately display an anomaly. It is not proof that the entire path was normal, nor can it settle the comparison involving `workspace package entrypoint`.

After seeing `workspace package entrypoint` at T+18, the old record described it as "hand off to the corresponding maintenance entry." The value of this sentence is that it records the first divergence: at least one comparison did not produce the same picture as the previous one. It did not provide a complete request that could be compared item by item, nor indicate whether the two states came from the object, the entry version, or the recording time.

When the user path recovered at T+31, the incident record did not fill in whether the requests before and after recovery were exactly the same. Recovery should therefore be written separately from cause confirmation. Previously treating the green result at the end of the timeline as the end of the incident was an overly broad reading; why the consumer regression changed along with it remains unanswered in this material.

## Gaps Not Filled by the Screenshot

EMRA-003 later reminded us that the before-and-after trends in the two versions of the record were not comparable because there was a change point in the entry. This reminder corrected one way of reading the record: the states or values before and after cannot be treated as a continuous change on the same baseline. It did not explain the two states as any specific fault.

The same card later contained only a screenshot; the original request corresponding to the exit entry was not attached. The screenshot can show that someone saw a discrepancy at a certain point in time, but it cannot reconstruct which entry the request passed through, nor prove that the screenshot was the original ember-client-integration input. Without the original request, the exit-entry result cannot be connected directly to the recovery at T+31.

The later green result also cannot overwrite the original incident context. This does not mean that green is invalid; it means that green belongs to later runtime conditions, while the initial anomaly occurred precisely when the recording time points were inconsistent. Green cannot replace the missing request, prove that the screenshot was wrong, or retroactively deny that the initial state discrepancy occurred.

## A Recovery Observation Cannot Become an Operational Conclusion

The initial record said that after owner destruction, the previously stuck path could recover. It did not say that owner destruction was the only change, nor that it applied to other call samples. Turning phenomena that occurred next to each other into operational steps would conceal a causal chain that was not present in the original record.

During the on-duty handoff, the recovery time and the root-cause confirmation time were not clearly separated, and later readers at one point treated "the last line was already green" as a strong attribution signal. Looking back, we can only narrow that statement: green is enough to show that there was no need at the time to keep watching that recovered path; it is not enough to answer for the original input where the change in consumer regression came from.

## The Public-Entry Review Was Split Apart

The action in EMRA-005 was to recheck the public entry using the original ember-client-integration; the local result served only as diagnostic material, so this retrospective does not write it up as a new substitute sample. The note left after the check began was: "I checked the on-duty person's run; I haven't tried the exit entry yet."

A further note was added: "I've finished checking the on-duty person's run; the user entry is waiting for another account." These statements cannot be consolidated into "the public environment has recovered." They only show that the on-duty person's run was compared, the exit entry had not yet been tried at that time, and the user entry was still waiting for another account. These three statuses are not the same thing.

The recovery of the user path at T+31 belongs to the original incident timeline; the material in EMRA-005 belongs to the subsequent public-entry review using the original input. The former does not prove that every direction of the public entry recovered, and the latter does not explain the source of the two states in the incident. Combining them would make readers think that the same input had already covered every entry point.

## The Original Input Cannot Be Replaced with a Similar Sample

EMRA-012 require replaying the original ember-client-integration for "@ember · Client Integration same object appears in two states," rather than rebuilding a similar input. This restriction preserves the association: the original input is a sample already directly linked to the anomaly, while a similar input, even if it runs successfully, may not pass through the adapter boundary that originally left the two-state record.

This does not mean that the original input is inherently more complete. The original record still lacks the original request corresponding to the exit entry; but if a similar input is substituted, the new input introduces new request conditions. If the new input does not show a discrepancy, that only means it does not show a discrepancy; it cannot be used to deny the old record.

EMRA-012 also contain the note "the expiration action still points to yesterday's object." There is no material here showing which object that action ultimately pointed back to, so it is not included in the cause. The card entering the in-progress state also does not provide a replay result; it only shows that the original input was still being treated as the object that needed to be used.

## Previous Conclusions That Still Apply

- Save the original input and entry version, and stop further retries. This is to separate the original incident context from later results, not a general integration procedure.
- When `Rollup input graph` is normal, this can only show that the point did not immediately display an anomaly at the time; it cannot settle `workspace package entrypoint`.
- Recovery of the path after owner destruction is a recovery observation, not a confirmed fix.
- After the user path recovers, the change in consumer regression remains an open item.

This page is being retained because the real call samples formed around @ember, the adapter boundary, and the integration feedback have their own schedule, maintainer, and exit criteria. The review entry remains `docs/adj-ember/incidents/ember-client-integration-two-states-for-one-object.md`. The uncertainties in the old record remain unchanged; runtime projects or conclusions from other integration work are not attached to this anomaly.

# Caller-Side Integration Debugging: Dual-State Anomaly Retrospective

The earliest sentence left on the page was "The same object appears in two states." Later, when someone returned here from an old link, they would often see this sentence first, followed by a user path that had already recovered, and connect two different things into a single conclusion: one was that the states seen at two recording points were inconsistent, and the other was that a call path no longer got stuck afterward. The original record did not prove that they had the same cause.

This retrospective did not clean up the old page into current documentation. It preserves the state differences visible at the time, the requests that were not fully captured, one recovery observation, and the entry points that remained separate in the subsequent review. The call samples, adapter boundaries, and integration feedback around @ember had their own schedule and maintenance scope; what is preserved here is that integration-debugging context, not a summary of the status of other projects.

The initial record only said that the current entry point reported different current revision values at two points in time. The old page did not contain enough material to show whether the two points shared the same complete request, nor did it show how much each of the object, entry version, and recording time contributed. The card material added later allowed several overly broad interpretations to be narrowed, but did not turn the cause into a definite answer.

## Where the Incident Stopped

The first thing noticed was that resolver registration was inconsistent with the old record. It was the easiest difference to see in the incident context, so someone discussed it as the cause. This was not an attribution confirmed later; at the time, all that had been seen was a different display, and no original material sufficient to compare the request conditions before and after had yet been obtained.

However, this old assessment is still worth leaving in its original place. It explains why retries were not continued at the time. If we had continued testing with new runs, the outputs produced afterward would have been mixed with the original record showing two states, making the meaning of "same object" on the page even harder to discern. Stopping further attempts and preserving the original input and entry version were the actions actually completed in this incident.

The storage location has always been:

`docs/adj-ember/incidents/ember-client-integration-two-states-for-one-object.md`

This entry contains the event record and the attachments left at the time. It preserves the limited fact that "one original input once left different state descriptions near the entry"; it did not preserve the complete request context, nor the complete conditions for the other normal path. New results later seen from the same path cannot automatically fill these gaps.

The first version also left two observations that should be read separately: after owner destruction, the path that had originally been stuck could recover; the reason the consumer regression changed was still unknown. The first was a result observed during recovery, while the second was an explicitly unresolved question. The two sentences were adjacent on the old page, making it easy to read the former as explaining the latter; in fact, there was no material linking object lifecycle, the destruction action, the recovery observation, and the consumer-side change into a causal chain.

The page also still had an unfilled blank at the time:

```text
Missing time point: ____
```

This was not later filled in with a precise clock time. What could later be organized was only the relative order of the fragments; the complete time point for each request could not be reconstructed. The blank was retained not to make the incident seem mysterious, but because this anomaly inherently involved whether the two records could be viewed under the same comparison conditions. Adding an ad hoc time would make the originally missing basis for comparison look as though it had existed.

## The Sequence Is Only a Collection of Incident Fragments

| Relative time | Record left at the time | Action taken at the time | What cannot be inferred from this row |
|---|---|---|---|
| T+00 | `ember-caller-side integration testing-same object appears in two states` deviated from the original record | Preserved the original input and entry-point version | The difference came from the object itself |
| T+07 | `Rollup input graph` remained normal | Did not expand the scope to all call samples | The entire call path was normal |
| T+18 | The comparison pointed to `workspace package entrypoint` | Left the divergence for the corresponding maintenance entry to investigate further | The requests on both sides were exactly identical |
| T+31 | One user path recovered | Kept recovery separate from root-cause confirmation | All entry points recovered |

T+00, T+07, T+18, and T+31 are the ordering used in the old materials, not times that can be stitched together with absolute clocks on other pages. Each row in the table preserves the local action taken at the time, but they do not form a complete continuous record from input to result. In particular, the material between T+00 and T+31 lacks evidence confirming that the request remained unchanged, so they cannot be treated as two snapshots before and after the same run.

The "two states" mentioned at T+00 also cannot be read retrospectively as the object first being in one definite state and then switching to another definite state. The old records support only the conclusion that the same object was presented differently in two sets of materials. The object itself, the entry-point version, the recording time, and the missing request context could all affect the interpretation; the team on site did not rule out these factors one by one.

The fact that `Rollup input graph` was normal at T+07 once narrowed the troubleshooting scope. It only shows that the diagram at that location did not immediately display an anomaly at the time. In the old draft, "still normal" was understood by some readers to mean that the integration testing as a whole was normal; it was later shown that this interpretation was too broad: one diagram showing no anomaly does not mean that all call samples, all entry points, or subsequent records showed no differences.

The `workspace package entrypoint` at T+18 was another comparison point. The old record read "routed to the corresponding maintenance entry"; what was actually left behind was the first divergence: at least one comparison did not produce the same picture as the preceding one. It did not include the complete request, so it cannot show that the two sides of the divergence came from the same environment, nor did it indicate whether the two states belonged respectively to the object, the entry-point version, or the recording time.

The recovery of the T+31 user path also needs to be read narrowly. The recovery indicates that this path was no longer stuck at that stage; it does not mean that all paths through the public entry point had been revalidated. Early pages placed the recovery at the end of the timeline, making it read as though the event had already ended; but the page never answered why the change in consumer regression appeared at the same time.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Call sample
    participant I as @ember integration debugging
    participant R as On-site record
    participant W as On-duty handler
    C->>I: Use original input
    I->>R: Record state discrepancy
    R-->>W: resolver registration differs
    W-->>R: Save version, do not retry further
    W-->>C: Path recovered, cause pending investigation
```

The diagram preserves the shortest interaction segment from the handling at that time. It does not depict the complete request, nor does it indicate that every call sample went through in the same order. The final arrow only places the recovery observation back in the on-site context; it is not confirmation of the root cause, much less proof that all entry points recovered. Missing request conditions, entry-point version, and recording time cannot be filled in by drawing the diagram.

## What the old screenshot can show

Early retellings included a screenshot. The screenshot can show that someone saw a state discrepancy at the time, but it cannot show where the request came in from, what revision the entry point used, why another path worked normally, or whether the screenshot corresponded to the original ember-client-integration input. It is a reference pointing to the on-site situation, not a complete request record.

EMRA-003 later left a more specific reminder: The before-and-after trends in the two versions of the records are not comparable; the point in time when the current entry point changed should be marked, and the before-and-after statistics should not be subtracted directly. This reminder corrected the comparison method. If the two materials do not share the same entry point and revision, changes in state or values before and after cannot be directly treated as a continuous trend on the same baseline.

This does not interpret the dual state as any particular failure. Even if the entry point's change point is known, the existing materials still cannot determine how much the object state, request conditions, and recording order each contributed. The fact that the entry point changed is a condition to note before comparison, not an alternative way of saying that the cause has been identified.

EMRA-003 later also recorded a handoff to someone else to continue handling it; the stated reason was that the main changes were in @ember · Client Integration's core module. This change only indicates that the focus of subsequent review remained near the integration target; it does not mean that the new handler had obtained the request that was initially missing, nor that the screenshot had been turned into a complete sample.

The card was later marked as blocked because it was waiting for upstream to provide publicly shareable samples. This wait was directly related to the limitations of the screenshots: without reusable original samples, looking back through the old links could only confirm what someone had once seen, not reconnect the exit entry point with the original request. The blocked status was not a judgment about the root cause, but only an indication that the materials needed to continue the comparison were missing at the time.

The same card also contains the line: "Only screenshots remain here; the original request corresponding to the exit entry point was not linked." What was missing was not some generic attachment, but the specific original request corresponding to the exit entry point. Therefore, even with the page and screenshots still available, it was impossible to piece together the exit entry point's results and the recovery at T+31, item by item, into a before-and-after comparison of the same request.

The old page once stated, "The green result after cleanup cannot overwrite the original incident state." That sentence is still retained, but its scope should be very narrow: the later green results are specific to the later run conditions and cannot replace the missing request or supply a common baseline for records from before the entry point change. This does not mean that the green results are invalid, much less that the screenshots are wrong; they simply cannot retroactively negate the fact that the initial difference in states occurred.

## resolver registration is not a confirmed cause

The initial working assessment was "resolver registration differs from the old records." In retrospect, this should be narrowed to "the first visible difference." At the time, this was the only signal sufficient to justify stopping further retries and preserving the incident state, and there was no evidence proving that it was the cause of the dual-state behavior.

This assessment was easy to overstate because it appeared both in the anomaly description and near the subsequent preservation actions. Readers could easily read "we stopped retrying because we saw that it was different" as "we found the cause because it was different." The former is a decision made during the incident, while the latter requires causal evidence; the original page contained only the former.

Retaining this old assessment also serves a practical purpose. If it were deleted, later readers would see an unexplained stop and an isolated entry point version, as if the person on duty had more information at the time. In fact, the opposite was true: they used the visible difference as a signal to stop precisely because it was no longer possible to safely compare new output.

Likewise, the observation that `Rollup input graph` was normal should not be turned into another attribution of cause. It was a local observation point, presented alongside `workspace package entrypoint`, not one of two interchangeable conclusions. The former did not immediately show an anomaly at the time, while the latter recorded a divergence; neither established a complete call chain.

The old materials at one point gave rise to the interpretation "`Rollup input graph` is normal, so the problem is not in integration testing." That claim later ceased to apply. A normal graph could only help narrow down where to look at the time, not support conclusions about other adaptation boundaries, other entry points, or the missing request context.

## Why the recovery observation was not documented as remediation steps

"After owner destruction, the previously stuck path can recover" is the sentence on this page most likely to be misused. It records two events that occurred in close succession: after the destruction-related actions, the previously stuck path showed recovery. The original record did not state that this was the only change between the states before and after recovery, nor did it state that other call samples, a different revision, or other entry points would produce the same result.

Therefore, this statement cannot be rewritten as reproducible handling steps, much less turned into an integration-testing conclusion that "executing owner destruction is enough for recovery". Doing so would turn an observation from the incident with gaps into a causal guarantee, obscuring what was not known in the first place.

During the early handoffs, the time of recovery and the time of root-cause confirmation were not clearly separated, and the final line of green output was once treated as a relatively strong signal for causal attribution. In hindsight, the meaning of green can only be narrowed: it indicated that there was no need at that point to keep watching the path that had already recovered; it cannot substitute for the original input in answering why consumer regression changed.

This also explains why the recovery page, the original record, and the unconfirmed cause were kept separately. The recovery page records that a path became available later, the original record preserves the input and the version around the entry point when the dual state appeared, and the unconfirmed cause preserves the gap between the two that the materials have not bridged. Collapsing these three types of material into a single "recovered incident" would make recovery look like an answer that was already known at the time.

## The public entry point recheck did not cover the same thing

The limited task for EMRA-005 was to recheck the public entry point using the original ember-client-integration, with local results used only to help locate the issue. This restriction matters: new local results can help narrow down where the problem is, but cannot replace the input and records associated with the original anomaly. The recheck is not about reconstructing a similar case, nor about writing a later successful sample back into the original incident.

After work began, the note left was: "I cross-checked the on-duty person's run; I haven't tried the exit entry point yet." This statement has two scope boundaries. The on-duty person's run was the specific area that had already been cross-checked; the exit entry point had not yet been tried. It cannot be read as either a failure of the exit entry point or a pass for the public entry point as a whole.

Another statement was added later: "I've finished cross-checking the on-duty person's run; the user entry point is waiting for another account." This is not a restatement of the previous sentence, but adds a third status for a specific area: the user entry point had not yet been compared under the same conditions. Waiting for another account does not mean an anomaly occurred at the user entry point, nor does it mean the results of the on-duty person's run can stand in for the user entry point.

In the original timeline, T+31 marks the recovery of the user path; EMRA-005 is material from the subsequent recheck of the public entry point using the original input. The former does not indicate that every branch of the public entry point had recovered, and the latter does not explain the origin of the dual state either. They are close in time and similar in name, but they are not the same complete verification.

If an earlier version assembled these fragments into "the public environment has recovered", that statement is inaccurate. The available materials support only this: the on-duty person's run had been cross-checked, the exit entry point had not been tried at the time, and the user entry point still depended on another account. This page has not filled in success or failure for the remaining branches.

The public entry point recheck also cannot replace the original request corresponding to the exit entry point. A subsequent comparison can show how one branch behaved under the conditions of that run, but does not automatically restore the associations missing from the original screenshot. Therefore, even if more green results are obtained later, the dual-state incident still needs to be read with the gaps in the original record in mind.

## The original input cannot be replaced with a similar sample

EMRA-012 requires replaying the original ember-client-integration for "@ember · Client Integration the same object appearing in two states," rather than reconstructing a similar input. What this requirement preserves is the existing relationship between the anomaly and the sample: the original input was once linked to the two-state record, whereas a similar input would introduce new request conditions.

Even if a similar input can run successfully, it does not necessarily pass through the original adapter boundary. It shows no difference; that only means it itself shows no difference, and cannot, in turn, disprove the old record. If the new input is treated as the answer for the old incident context, the page will show a comparison that looks complete but actually uses a different object.

This does not mean the original input is inherently complete. The original record is still missing the original request corresponding to the exit endpoint, and preserving the original input does not automatically supply all request conditions. The value of the original input is not that "it must explain the event," but that it has a direct relationship to the anomaly that occurred; replacing it would lose that relationship.

EMRA-012 contains a note that "the expiration action still points back to yesterday's object." There is no evidence here showing which object the expiration action should ultimately point back to, so we do not fold it into the cause or characterize it as either replay success or replay failure. It only suggests that the targets of replay-related actions may already be stale.

The card later had its on-call schedule rearranged and its assignee changed, after which it entered an in-progress state. These changes indicate that the replay work was still in the queue; they do not provide an actual replay result. Writing the task status as a verification result would repeat the initial confusion in this incident: mistaking a page state for an object state.

The constraints on the original input also explain why we do not propose substituting a "close enough" case here. Close does not mean the same input; once the input conditions change, differences that appear or do not appear at the adapter boundary cannot be directly used to explain the old incident context.

## What the entry point, revision, and exit request each leave behind

The entry version records the version near the entry point corresponding to a particular observation. It can prevent later results from directly overwriting the initial record, but it is not a baseline shared by the two time points. The two time points show different current revision values; this is precisely the context for the reminder in EMRA-003 that the earlier and later records cannot be directly subtracted from each other.

A screenshot records the visible state at a particular point in time. It can support "a difference was once observed," but not "where the difference originated." A screenshot does not contain the complete request, so it cannot reconstruct which entry point the input came through or explain the state of the other path.

The issue with the exit endpoint is different: what is missing is its mount relationship to the original request. The exit endpoint may still be described and accessed, and may even have subsequent results; but if we cannot confirm which original request it corresponds to, we cannot put it and the original two-state record in the same comparison group.

`Rollup input graph` records a normal observation, while `workspace package entrypoint` records another branching point. They are not the same kind of evidence, nor does either draw a conclusion on behalf of the other. The former cannot override the latter, and the latter does not, in turn, prove that the former is wrong.

The recovery page documents the fact that the user path later recovered. It does not include the original request from the exit entry point, nor does it fill the gap while the user entry point was waiting for another account. The original record, the recovery page, and the unconfirmed cause are kept separate not to create more entry points, but because they answer different local questions.

## Statements that were previously interpreted too broadly

### "resolver registration is the root cause"

This no longer applied later. What can be retained is its status as the first visible difference; it cannot be elevated to a complete causal attribution. The available material does not establish a verifiable causal relationship among resolver registration, the dual states, entry point versions, and consumer regression.

### "`Rollup input graph` is normal, so the problem is not in integration testing"

This is also an overly broad interpretation. A normal graph can only narrow the scope of observation at the time; it cannot rule out differences before or after `workspace package entrypoint` or at other adaptation boundaries. The old record does not contain a complete call chain, so one normal observation cannot be used to infer that everything was normal.

### "owner destruction is the recovery method"

We should return to the original wording: the path recovered after owner destruction. Events occurring close together do not automatically establish a fixed action-and-outcome relationship. No material shows that other call samples, different current revision values, or different entry points would produce the same result.

### "The public entry point has been fully rechecked"

Subsequent card material shows that this conclusion was inaccurate. When the person on duty had finished that round of checks, the exit entry point had not yet been tried, and the user entry point was still waiting for another account. These three local states should not be compressed into a single complete recheck.

### "Similar input can replace the original input"

This does not apply to this replay. Similar input has no history directly connected to the anomaly and cannot confirm or refute the state differences left when the original input passed through the adaptation boundary. The restriction in EMRA-012 preserves the link to the incident context rather than adding another set of steps.

## The impact remained confined to the integration-testing target

This anomaly involved real call samples, adaptation boundaries, and integration feedback that emerged around @ember. The integration-testing project has its own schedule, maintainer, and exit criteria, so similar changes in the runtime project or other adjacent projects cannot be included directly in this postmortem, nor can results from elsewhere replace the missing parts of the original input.

The impact window is not quantified on this page. The available material supports only the following description: the same target appears in different states in two records; one user path recovered during that period; the public entry point's rechecks were not all completed under the same conditions. A broader scope would require material that clearly correlates requests, revision values, and entry points; none is available here.

The repeated target name in the title must not be read as two independent targets either. It refers to the same integration-testing target as presented in different records. The page does not contain enough information to determine whether the difference came from the target itself, the entry point version, the time of recording, or missing request context; any early attribution of the cause to one of these alone can only be considered a working judgment at the time.

Nor can this record alone determine whether subsequent replay can end after one user path has recovered. This page only preserves the distinction between the recovery observation and the unconfirmed cause; it does not determine completion for the exit entry point, public entry point, or user entry point.

## Materials Still Available for Review

When you need to revisit the incident state, continue to use `docs/adj-ember/incidents/ember-client-integration-two-states-for-one-object.md` as the entry point. This path can retrieve the original record and attachments, but does not guarantee that the original request for the exit entry point has been supplied in full, nor does it guarantee that the complete state from that time can still be retrieved now. Its purpose is to return to the preserved incident state, not to replace historical records with current results.

EMRA-003 preserve the timing of the entry point change and the reminder that records from before and after cannot be directly compared. EMRA-005 preserve the fact that the public entry point recheck was split up. EMRA-012 preserve the restriction that the original ember-client-integration replay cannot be replaced with similar samples. Each of the three cards fills in only one part, and they cannot be combined into "the root cause has been fully established".

As for the assessments that were not deleted from the old page, they should not be mistaken for the current interpretation either. resolver registration was once treated as the cause, `Rollup input graph` was once treated as a signal for narrowing the scope, and owner destruction once accompanied recovery; these are all genuine traces preserved from the incident, but each retains only its original explanatory scope.

## Unconfirmed Items

- Whether the two states come from the same complete request context, unconfirmed;
- The relationship between the change in consumer regression and the observed recovery, unconfirmed;
- The original request corresponding to the exit entry point has not been linked;
- Whether the account the user entry point was waiting on ultimately completed a recheck under the same conditions, not recorded;
- Why the expiration action mentioned in EMRA-012 still points to yesterday's object, unconfirmed;
- Whether the difference between the two current revision values is sufficient to explain the different states, unconfirmed.

These gaps reflect the retained material more faithfully than a tidy attribution of cause. When citing this page later, first distinguish whether you are looking at the original input and initial records, recovery along the user path, a partial recheck of the public entry point, or pending items for replaying the original input; they may be related, but should not be treated as the same complete verification merely because they share the same title.

# Alternative Approaches for Caller Integration

At the time, @ember's caller integration was stuck on one narrow point of disagreement: whether the failure exits should continue to be folded into the existing result, or whether a separate compatibility layer should be left outside `ember-client-integration`. This comparison covers two approaches that have not yet been implemented; neither is presented as an existing rule.

One approach continues to use `standalone render result`. It leaves the existing integration method unchanged, at the cost of keeping the two failure exit paths lumped together. The other approach splits `compatibility boundary` out on its own, giving callers a clear place to look when crossing the boundary; but before doing that, we must know exactly which callers are using `workspace package entrypoint`.

I tentatively favor separating the boundary, because the two failure exit paths in the source material at `docs/adj-ember/proposals/unused-ember-client-integration-approach.md` are not the same. That difference is not enough to establish that the split is necessarily correct: the caller Fang Ke may simply be reusing the same entry point, or may depend on the shape of the merged result.

Whether reverting can be done just by restoring the old entry point is still unresolved. If the split requires more changes to existing callers than expected, it should no longer be treated as a localized cleanup. First retain the original entry point and this comparison, then decide whether to try the split once the full scope of callers has been established.

# Alternative Approach for Caller Integration Testing

The original proposal to extract a compatibility layer was not intended to create a separate entry point for caller integration testing. The case at hand already had `standalone render result`, and the two failure exits in `ember-client-integration` appeared different. The question then was whether callers actually needed an identifiable `compatibility boundary`, or just needed to keep receiving the existing result.

This approach was later dropped. Not because a later implementation proved it wrong, but because the records used to assess it were not reliable enough: some case records mixed together the expiry action, the result currently shown on the page, and the original failure. Using those materials in the extraction proposal would only disguise a record-timing issue as an interface-boundary issue.

## The two options compared at the time

Keeping `standalone render result` meant callers would not have to change entry points immediately. It also had a clear gap: when two failure exits converged on the same result, readers of the records would have difficulty telling whether an exception occurred before caller adaptation or was merged afterward.

The idea behind extracting `compatibility boundary` was the opposite. There would be a specific point to locate when a caller crossed the boundary, and the two failure exits could leave separate traces. The cost was that once the boundary became part of the entry point, existing callers of `workspace package entrypoint` could no longer be treated as unknown background. Migration, rollback, and the scope of retaining the old entry point would all need to be defined first.

The first draft favored the second option based only on the difference between the failure exits. That was a working hypothesis, not a result. It did not answer whether callers actually depended on the merged result, or whether restoring only the old entry point would be enough for rollback.

## Evidence withdrawn after review

Subsequent records in EMRA-002 showed that one expiry action had been sent to the wrong card and did not belong to the same case as this rejected approach. That action could therefore no longer be used to prove that a caller had chosen the split at a particular point in time, or to establish the order of the proposals.

EMRA-004 made the issue more specific: the only attachments at the time were screenshots, and the original failure had not yet been obtained. The result shown on the page then changed a second time, while the expiry action still retained the old value. Screenshots can show what the page displayed at one point, but they cannot replace the original failure, much less establish that the second page change reflected a difference between the two candidate approaches.

These two additions changed how the evidence could be used; they did not rewrite the old draft as though the answer had been known all along. The original observation that "the two failure exits differ" remained the reason for raising the question. The proposal was later withdrawn because it could not withstand the ambiguity introduced by the timing issues and missing original material described above.

## The approach not adopted

In this round, we will not split `compatibility boundary` into an independent integration path, or require callers to move away from `standalone render result`. Retaining the existing entry point has a limited meaning: until caller scope and the original failures have been filled in, a structural change must not become a promise of compatibility behavior.

This is not a permanent rejection of the split. Before reopening the discussion, the material should at least be able to answer two questions: which existing callers go through `workspace package entrypoint`, and what original failure corresponds to each of the two failure exits. If all we have is page screenshots or a single green result, the discussion should stay at the record level and not move into entry-point migration.

The review also required retaining one contrasting input to test whether "the two exits differ" was merely an apparent difference caused by input conditions. That input has not yet been turned into a concrete sample. Until the sample, caller feedback, and entry-point scope are all available, a new trial must not be described as having started.

## Rollback and open items

If someone later attempts the split ahead of this, they should stop if they cannot explain the scope of rollback to the old entry point, or if the new boundary requires callers to make adaptation changes that have not been listed. Whether rollback requires only a return to the old entry point remains undecided. This is precisely a question the first draft left open, not one that has since been filled in as a conclusion.

The related cases can be revisited through EMRA-002 and EMRA-004. For the migration index, see DOC-33. This page records only why this rejected approach was proposed, why it was withdrawn, and what is missing before the discussion can be reopened.

# Quality Signal Handoff Troubleshooting Tree

When the quality signal console gets stuck, don't immediately attribute it to a particular test or entry point. Gather the current entry point, the first failure output, and the logs from the same test run; retain trace or diff excerpts too, if available. If any of these items is missing from the evidence, collect it first; do not assess the cause.

```text
Start: node-tests-quality-signal is stuck
│
├─ Original output missing
│  └─ Collect it; do not hand off without the first failing sample
│
├─ Original output available, but the same-named signal has no version identifier
│  └─ Record the old and current objects separately; do not substitute adjacent records
│
├─ Signal and entry point can be matched
│  ├─ First difference appears only in the project's own input or output
│  │  └─ Keep investigating in node tests · Quality Signal Board
│  └─ Difference requires changing permissions, confirming an exit action, or crossing a defined interface
│     └─ Hand off to the responsible maintainers with the captured evidence
│
└─ Green after a rerun
   └─ Retain the original failing sample; green does not establish recovery
```

For same-named `node-tests-quality-signal` objects, don't rely on the name alone. First check whether the object and the current entry point appear together, then check whether the references include a version. EMRB-009 recorded missing version identifiers for same-named objects; in this situation, adding the identifiers is more useful than continuing to compare outputs. If the objects haven't been separated, subsequent differences can easily end up associated with an old sample.

If the records are complete, compare only the first difference between the most recent normal sample and the failing sample. Keep the current entry point unchanged during the comparison, and swap only the adjacent signal inputs. EMRB-003 previously involved preparations for a replay along these lines, but the available samples could not distinguish between the two cases, and the investigation ended immediately afterward. So retain the candidate differences here; do not write up a replay that could not distinguish the cases as a conclusion.

When the inputs, test logs, and outputs all fall within the quality signal console's own scope, continue investigating the causes of unstable signals. Change only one comparison condition at a time; if a second condition also needs to change, save a separate sample first. When rerunning, it should still be possible to tell which objects were actually compared when it first got stuck.

A common mistake is to clean things up before retrying. Older records show this happening: only green results remained afterward, leaving no way to tell whether the stall was related to environment differences. Now save the original input, version information, and first output before deciding whether to rerun. If the rerun is still stuck, append the new output; if it turns green, place that green result after the original failing sample as well.

A handoff does not mean handing over the entire investigation. Include only the current entry point, the two objects being compared, the first failure output, and confirmed environment differences in the handoff material. If the issue is permissions, state which permission needs confirmation; if the issue is an exit action, state the step where local work has stopped. Without new evidence, do not follow the tree beyond the interface boundary.

EMRB-002 was previously held up because the maintenance window had closed, then canceled because it duplicated an implementation card under the same document. A change in card status changes how the work is tracked; it does not invalidate the original failing sample. The records before handback only listed the person on duty, and part of the output from the exit entry point was missing; explicitly note the missing output in future handoffs.

The maintenance location is still `docs/adj-node-tests/runbooks/node-tests-quality-signal-escalation-contacts.md`.
