# Quality Signal Handoff Troubleshooting Tree

When the Quality Signal Console gets stuck, first preserve the state as it was first observed. Here, "first" means the symptoms actually displayed at the current entry point and the records that can be matched to them before rerunning, cleaning up, or replacing adjacent signal inputs. Keep the failure output, test logs from the same run, and any obtainable trace excerpts or diff excerpts together. It is not uncommon for a subsequent run to turn green; that is a new sample and must not overwrite the initial failure record.

Sometimes only screenshots or old links remain. Screenshots can help locate the page being viewed at the time, and old links can point to the original record location, but neither is the raw output. They often do not show whether a same-named signal points to an old object or the current object, nor do they show what input the entry point had at the time. Look for the output and logs first; if they cannot be found, note which record is missing, then stop at the corresponding branch.

```text
node-tests-quality-signal is stuck
│
├─ No raw output or test logs from the same run
│  └─ Collect the missing data; do not assess the cause or hand off yet
│
├─ Records exist, but same-named signals have no version identifiers
│  └─ Distinguish the old object from the current object, then continue
│
├─ The entry point and signal can be matched
│  ├─ Compared with the most recent normal sample, the first difference is still within the project
│  │  └─ Stay with the Quality Signal Console and continue investigating unstable signals
│  ├─ The first difference appears only on the environment side
│  │  └─ Preserve the difference and wait for new input, logs, or output
│  └─ Permissions need to change, or the exit action requires confirmation from outside the interface
│     └─ Organize the current evidence, then hand off
│
└─ Turns green after a rerun
   └─ Save the green result separately as a new sample; do not delete the original failed sample
```

## Distinguish Same-Named Objects First

`node-tests-quality-signal` is a starting point for troubleshooting, not a sufficient object identifier. When same-named records are mixed together, first check whether the signal appeared at the same time as the current entry point, then check whether the reference specifies a version. EMRB-009 tracked missing version identifiers for same-named objects; the problem at the time was not a lack of output, but that the old object and the current object could not be distinguished by name alone.

Troubleshooting the current stall does not require filling in all historical records. At a minimum, it must be possible to say which object the failed sample references and which object the most recent normal sample references. If neither is clear, add identifiers first; if only one side has been identified, remain at this branch. Do not substitute adjacent records for a missing object, and do not put two objects into the same comparison just because their names match.

If output exists but the objects have not yet been distinguished, do not compare output details yet. Those details may be clues to the stall, or they may simply be natural differences produced by different objects. Note the version information gap alongside the sample, preserve the originals, and continue only once the entry point and object can be matched. At this stage, working backward from the final display to infer what happened in between can easily attribute an old object's results to the current object.

If the page contains only a signal name and a summary, first treat that summary as a clue for locating the records, not as the sample itself. A summary cannot replace the input and output it omits. If someone later obtains the full logs, append them after the original locating clue rather than rewriting the old summary as though it already contained all the fields at the time.

## Change Only One Variable When Comparing

Once the objects can be matched, take the most recent normal sample and find the earliest difference between it and the failed sample. Keep the current entry point unchanged and replace only the adjacent signal input. This comparison produces a candidate difference: it indicates where to look next, but does not mean the cause of the stall has already been explained.

EMRB-003 prepared to verify the issue by replaying adjacent inputs, but the investigation later ended because the available samples could not distinguish between two situations. This is not a record of "no anomalies", but a record of an investigation that lacked enough material to continue distinguishing between them. In the same situation, do not change the entry point, environment, and second input simultaneously to obtain a green result; preserve the candidate difference and note what type of record is still missing.

If the first difference is in the Quality Signal Console's own input, test logs, or output, continue troubleshooting within the project. You can add a new sample that changes only one condition, or organize unstable signals by their failure symptoms; whichever approach you use, keep the first failed sample alongside the comparison results. Averaged results cannot explain a specific stall.

If a second condition must also change, do not add it to the same comparison. Keep a separate sample and note that it is no longer a single-variable controlled comparison. If you later see a green result, you will still be able to distinguish whether it came from a change in the adjacent signal input or a change in the entry point or environment. If even the entry point has changed in the new sample, that sample may only be used to discover new issues, not to backfill the original comparison's conclusions.

The purpose of the most recent normal sample is to establish a comparison baseline, not to replace the failed sample. Even a very complete final state in the normal sample cannot fill in intermediate output that was not saved in the failed sample. If either record lacks an object identifier, return to the object branch first rather than continuing to compare the text at the end of the output.

## Preserve Environmental Differences Before Naming a Cause

Different environments only mean that the current comparison is not yet aligned; they do not automatically mean that the environment is the cause. First preserve the differences already observed and specify which failure output, test log, or entry-point record they appear in. If new input, logs, or output cannot be obtained, stop here in the tree; do not reconstruct the intermediate process from directory names, the page's final state, or a new successful run.

Older records included a practice of cleaning up the state before rerunning. When the rerun turned green, only the successful result and scattered recollections remained, making it impossible to confirm later whether the input, environment, and output were the same before the stall. The order is now reversed: save the first failed sample, then decide whether to rerun.

If the rerun still gets stuck, append the new failure output after the original sample and preserve the conditions that actually changed between the two runs. If the rerun turns green, keep the green record too, but label it as a new sample. A green result can help determine whether more data collection is needed; it does not allow the evidence from the previous stall to be deleted.

Do not clear the state when the maintenance window ends either. EMRB-002 was blocked because the window closed, then later canceled because it duplicated an implementation card under the same document. These two status changes adjusted how the issue was tracked; they do not mean the original failed sample is no longer valid. After the window ends, the preserved entry point, object identifiers, and output can still be used to determine what needs to be collected next.

If the environmental difference remains the earliest inconsistency found, and no new record can separate it from the input, do not put "environment issue" in the handoff title. The handoff material only needs to state that the comparison is not yet aligned and what type of record is currently missing. This prevents the receiving party from treating a difference awaiting verification as a confirmed cause attribution.

## Exit Point for Keeping the Investigation Within the Project

As long as the first difference is still in the Quality Signal Console's own input, test logs, or output, stay within the project for now. There is no need to label the failure immediately; the priority is to preserve the state so it can be compared again. Keep the input, output, and environmental differences alongside the record from the same run, so that a fragment of output is not all that remains later, with its entry point forgotten.

When continuing the investigation within the project, do not merge multiple stalls into one sample just because their symptoms are similar. For each occurrence, preserve at least its own first failure output; if a later occurrence is the result of a rerun or replacement of an adjacent input, also note its relationship to the previous occurrence. This avoids incorrectly recording a stall in a different environment as a continuous failure of the same signal.

Once same-named objects have been distinguished, the entry point can be matched, and the single-variable comparison points within the project, this handoff process can end while local investigation into the causes of unstable signals continues. Ending here only means that assistance from outside the interface is not needed; it does not mean the root cause has been confirmed, nor does it require making definitive statements in place of environmental records that have not been obtained.

## Two Situations Requiring an External Handoff

There are only two situations in which troubleshooting leaves the local scope: permissions need to change, or the exit action requires confirmation from a maintainer outside the interface. Before handing off, organize a snapshot sufficient for someone else to take over, without retelling the entire troubleshooting history: the symptoms actually displayed at the current entry point, the objects corresponding to the failed and normal samples respectively, the first failure output, confirmed environmental differences, completed single-variable comparisons, and the point where the investigation stopped.

"Permission confirmation needed" must specify exactly which confirmation is missing, rather than leaving only a handoff marker. "Exit action unconfirmed" must also specify which node in the tree the local investigation stopped at. The receiving party can then decide whether to collect missing output, add object identifiers, or handle actions within their own scope first; they cannot be expected to infer the original branch from a green result after a rerun.

A handback record once listed only the person on duty, and a section of the output from the exit entry point was missing. Even after this gap was included in EMRB-009, it still could not be considered filled. In future handoffs, incomplete output does not prevent an external handoff, but the section that has not been obtained must be explicitly identified so the receiving party does not mistakenly assume that all the evidence has been seen.

When a temporary takeover sequence is involved, use the mapping in DOC-37 to confirm who takes on the current action. This page retains only symptoms, samples, comparison conditions, and stopping points; it does not adjust the boundaries of temporary takeovers here.

Routine maintenance remains in `docs/adj-node-tests/runbooks/node-tests-quality-signal-escalation-contacts.md`. Each time a record is added, first add it to the corresponding branch rather than inserting a new sample into an old object's description. Materials and attachments in the path are kept by node tests · Quality Signal Board; when referencing same-named signals, include whatever version information can be obtained.

This tree has two practical exits: a single-variable comparison within the project has produced a difference sufficient to continue the work, or the handoff material specifies the current entry point, sample-to-object mappings, output gaps, and items requiring confirmation. If there is no raw output, same-named objects have not been distinguished, or the next step depends on new records that have not yet been obtained, stop at the corresponding node and resume once new material becomes available.

# type tests Temporary Takeover Boundaries

This page initially tried to address temporary coverage gaps with "who to contact now", but it later became clear that the unassigned slots were actually the easiest part of the table to overlook: someone's ability to handle an action when it comes due does not mean they have taken over explaining behavior. After the second version separated the entry points, navigation breaks and revision comparisons also started coming in through the same place. This version retains that separation and puts the material each card can provide back within the corresponding responsibility boundaries.

The temporary maintainer only handles exit actions when they come due; explanations of the behavior of type-tests-package-integration still go back to the original owner, and unassigned slots remain visible.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Question received about the current revision] --> B{First confirm what the issue is}
    B -->|Exit action is due| C[Temporary maintainer handles the current action]
    B -->|Behavior explanation| D[Original owner]
    B -->|Navigation break| E[Actual consumer records the first broken-link location]
    E --> F[Temporary maintainer forwards the entry point and observations]
    F --> D
    B -->|Long-term maintainer not confirmed| G[Unassigned slot remains in the responsibility table]
    C --> H{Has the issue become one of explaining behavior}
    H -->|Yes| D
    H -->|No| I[Finish the current due action]
```

## An Entry Point Is Not an Ownership Claim

`docs/adj-type-tests/ownership/adj-type-tests-temporary-handover-boundaries.md` is the handoff entry point for type tests · Package Integration Collaboration. It lets people asking questions find the current handler and lets the temporary maintainer see which slots still lack stable ownership; it does not mean that every object appearing under that directory is assigned to the temporary maintainer.

In the first version, "temporary takeover" was defined too broadly, making it easy to push two different kinds of requests onto one person. Now, first ask what the request needs: if it only needs an exit action handled when it comes due, the temporary maintainer can take it on; if the request requires explaining the behavior of type-tests-package-integration, tracing where that behavior originated, or determining whether a difference represents a cross-package semantic change, it goes to the original owner. Even if the latter questions stem from the same navigation break, their responsibility assignments should not be rewritten just because they share an entry point.

| Request or object | Initial handler | What is passed to this handler | Responsibility boundary |
|---|---|---|---|
| Handling an exit action when due | Temporary maintainer | Current action and its due status | Do not explain cross-package behavior |
| Meaning of the behavior of type-tests-package-integration | Original owner | Specific behavior question and observed symptoms | Do not treat the temporary takeover record as a conclusion |
| Source tracing | Original owner | Available revision clues | Do not infer the source from displayed text |
| Navigation break in the current revision | Actual consumer records it first, temporary maintainer forwards it | First broken-link location after entering through the entry point | Do not assign a long-term owner based on the break location |
| Adjacent revision comparison | Temporary maintainer organizes the case details | One traversable path and the first path difference | Do not infer a behavior change from this difference |
| Unconfirmed long-term maintenance assignment | Unassigned slot | Known object name and the gap | Do not fill in the name of the most recent respondent |

## Material Provided by the Cards

The scope recorded in EMRC-001 is "designate only the person taking over the current action". It therefore supports the temporary maintainer in handling the due action, but does not transfer the long-term maintenance responsibility along with it. After handling is complete, the unassigned slot in the table should still remain; the temporary maintainer must not be relabeled as the long-term owner just because the action is complete.

EMRC-003 is used to compare link paths for adjacent current revisions. When comparing, choose one traversable path and compare only the first point where the paths differ. "First" matters here: it is location information that makes the case details easier to hand off, not an explanation of behavior. If interpreting what the dependencies between packages mean is needed after that difference, pass the material together with the current revision to the original owner, without adding inferences to the takeover table.

The goal of EMRC-006 is to trace back through the revisions of type-tests-package-integration to the earliest source that can be reconstructed. The text displayed on the page may be a later result, and cannot be used to work backward to a conclusion about the source. The temporary maintainer can provide the current entry point and existing broken-link records; source tracing itself is continued by the original owner, because it returns to the scope of responsibility for explaining behavior.

EMRC-008 starts with the actual consumer: have the consumer enter from the current revision and record the first broken-link location. This record should be forwarded unchanged with the handoff, because it shows the step at which navigation lost continuity. It does not explain the cause, nor does it say which package must take over the fix. If there is no consumer record, do not fill in an assumed broken-link location in the responsibility table.

## Where Temporary Handling Stops

After receiving a request, the temporary maintainer first preserves the current revision and the minimum observations. For navigation issues, the minimum observations are where the consumer entered and where the first break occurred; for adjacent revision comparisons, they are one traversable path and the first point of difference. When information is insufficient, handling can stop at an unassigned slot or a record of observations, with no need to fill in a complete account of the behavior just to make the handoff.

In the following situations, stop temporary handling immediately and return the issue to the original owner:

- The request starts asking why type-tests-package-integration behaves as it does;
- Differences in a revision need to be interpreted as cross-package dependency changes;
- Source tracing is no longer about locating the entry point, but instead requires determining the meaning of the earliest source;
- Someone asks for a long-term owner to be assigned directly based on old links, page text, or the most recent reply.

"Stop" does not mean the issue is abandoned. The temporary maintainer still passes the current revision, first path difference, or first broken-link location already obtained to the original owner; the unassigned slot remains in the table and is updated only once there is an explicit acceptance of ownership. This way, exit actions can be completed on time, and explanations of behavior will not lose their original context because of the temporary takeover.

## Unassigned Slots Still Awaiting Confirmation

There is currently no material identifying a long-term maintainer for `type-tests-package-integration`. This gap is different from "who can forward the entry point": the former requires an explicit long-term ownership claim, while the latter is only a relay role in the current collaboration. EMRC-001, EMRC-003, EMRC-006 and EMRC-008 can help supply action details, paths, source clues, and broken-link locations, respectively, but none can independently name a responsible person for the unassigned slot.

Therefore, if someone later brings up a similarly named package, an old link, or a record of a particular reply, first check whether it actually answers the question of long-term ownership. If it does not, attach it only to the relevant case details, and leave the unassigned slot in this table unchanged.

# Runtime Observability Entry Point Migration Guide

Runtime signals, failure context, and recovery observation windows for blueprints were originally accessed through a set of old entry points. Don't treat them as the same kind of record during migration: `resolver registration` and `owner destruction` have different failure exit points. Keep the former at the registration-related replacement location and record the latter separately. Mixing them together makes it easy to mistake recovery observations for registration errors.

The index file is at `docs/adj-blueprints/migration/current-entry-legacy-entry-migration-index.md`. It retains the old entry points, replacement locations, and active callers; explanations that cannot be traced back remain marked as outdated. Don't fill in explanations based on similar names. A new entry point appearing in the directory only shows that navigation has been added, not that migration is complete.

## Migration Order

1. First retrieve an actual incident record from an old entry point and confirm whether it describes runtime signals, failure context, or a recovery observation window.
2. Cross-check against the failure exit points. Move content about the registration process to the `resolver registration` side; move content involving object destruction to the `owner destruction` side. Don't merge them just because both entry points point to blueprints.
3. At the replacement location, keep the link to the original entry point and the existing dates so that anyone reviewing the old failure context can still return to the original record. Stop adding new explanations to the old entry point.
4. Confirm, one by one, whether each active caller has switched to the replacement location. Base confirmation on actual consumers, not filenames, directory hierarchy, or new links in the index.
5. Leave unconfirmed callers in the index. `consumer regression` currently has no verifiable active callers; that is not grounds for declaring the migration complete.

## Return to the Old Entry Point

If recovery observations cannot be matched to a separate failure exit point after migration, first stop moving any more records of that kind and return to the old entry point to check the original failure context. Restore navigation to the old entry point at that stage; don't rewrite the meaning of old records in the process. Wait for caller confirmation before deciding whether to rerun the migration. Whether to restore only the old entry point without withdrawing the replacement location still needs to be judged based on usage at the time.

# Beta Branch Cut Decision Record

The beta branch cut review involves two actions that are easily conflated: where to access the existing build-tooling, and which changes can enter the backport window. They are close in time, but the criteria for deciding them differ. The entry point determines which existing location maintainers start reviewing from; the window determines whether a particular migration can be accepted in this round. Moving both the entry point and the window at once makes the record look tidy, but does not necessarily preserve the relationships between the evidence.

The decision for this round is to retain the current build-tooling entry point. The backport window does not expand because the entry point remains available, nor does it receive default approval because the cut has already started. The maintenance materials for Ember.js Core must first arrange the build, generator, and runtime evidence into a causal chain on the same baseline, before determining whether a migration can be merged. When the evidence covers only one segment, approval extends only to that segment.

"Adjust the window" has not been deleted. It remains in the record as an option that was not adopted, not because adjusting the window is necessarily wrong in itself, but because it reverses the order: move the boundary first, then look for materials that can explain build changes, generator output, and runtime behavior. This order makes it easy to misread "available for review" as "already proven suitable for backporting".

## The Two Options on the Table During Review

| Option | Treatment in this round | Assessment at the time |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Retain the current build-tooling entry point | Adopted | Continue organizing materials from the same baseline at the existing location, avoiding simultaneous changes to the search starting point and the migration boundary. |
| Adjust the backport window | Not the default path | The window can only define the candidate scope; it cannot replace the still-missing links between the build, generator, and runtime. |

Adopting the first option does not mean recognizing the current entry point as the permanent home. Review materials were previously located using `packages/@ember/array/index.ts` and related call names. This path was only the starting point for review at the time; no decision was made to elevate it to the home for the branch cut or long-term maintenance. Retaining the entry point gives this round of decisions a stable starting point, rather than deciding all future changes in advance.

The second option offers a practical convenience: adjusting the window uniformly first would make subsequent backports more straightforward to describe. But that convenience depends on a premise the materials have not yet established: that all parts proposed for migration can be explained by the three types of evidence in relation to one another on the same baseline. This round did not fill that gap with speculation, nor did it treat a tidy window boundary as a compatibility conclusion.

## How the Evidence Chain Affects the Approval Scope

The same baseline must be fixed first, and the materials from the three areas then reviewed separately. The build side explains where inputs and outputs reside; the generator side explains how the generated content changes as a result; the runtime side explains how those changes manifest during execution. "Separately" here does not mean simply adding three sets of results together, but being able to explain how a change in one area leads to the next.

If only build materials are available, the conclusion remains limited to the build side. If generator materials exist but cannot be traced back to the same baseline, they cannot be borrowed to fill a gap in another migration either. Similar behavior at runtime likewise cannot, on its own, prove that all changes within the window meet the conditions for merging. Approval granularity is divided according to the scope actually covered by the evidence, not the overall progress of this round's cut.

This is also why the "not adopted" option is retained. It records not just the outcome, but also why the review did not choose to change the boundary first. If new materials become available later, the options can be compared again; that comparison must identify which segment of the build, generator, or runtime chain has been filled in, rather than merely saying that the window is more convenient.

## Sequence in the CI Record

The shared CI maintenance materials left this requirement:

> Shared CI maintenance preserves the first failed job and records any environment-only rerun difference.

The first failed job must be preserved. It marks the first place where a problem surfaced on the same baseline and cannot be overwritten because a later rerun produced a different result. If a rerun changes only the environment, the environment differences must also be saved alongside the first failure. This makes it possible to distinguish the original failure from the result after the environment changed, rather than treating "rerun" as a single state.

The reading order for maintainers is therefore clear: first confirm which job failed first, then examine what subsequent reruns changed, and finally place those differences back into the relationships between the build, generator, and runtime. Environment changes can explain why a particular result differs, but cannot replace generator or runtime materials on their own. A passing rerun also cannot automatically erase the earliest failure.

This recording requirement is not an additional release procedure. It preserves the chronological order needed for the assessment: which job failed first, which difference appeared only later, and whether that difference is sufficient to change the understanding of the same baseline. If only the final CI status is retained, the window assessment cannot distinguish the original failure from changes introduced by the maintenance environment.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Retain the current build-tooling entry point] --> B[Fix the same baseline]
  I[First failed job] --> B
  J[Environment-only rerun difference] --> B
  B --> C[Build materials]
  C --> D[Generator materials]
  D --> E[Runtime materials]
  E --> F{Is the evidence chain connected}
  F -->|Yes| G[Approve only the covered scope]
  F -->|No| H[Do not expand the backport window]
```

## Objections Retained from the Review

Some used "the entry point remains available" as a reason to adjust the window first. This reasoning was not adopted, because an available entry point only means that materials can still be reviewed starting from that location, not that runtime compatibility has been verified. Another tendency was to treat the generator as an adjunct to the build results and skip it as long as the build showed no obvious anomalies. This practice was also retained as a counterexample: it would leave a segment of changes between the build and runtime without anything that could be inspected.

Neither of these arguments was deleted from the decision. They explain why this round did not seek to broaden the window all at once, and why "retain the current entry point" is not preapproval for all subsequent migrations. The reasons for not adopting an option must remain with that option; otherwise, anyone later seeing only the final state of the entry point and window would be unable to reconstruct the boundaries of the assessment at the time.

## The Order Actually Used During the Cut

For a migration being prepared to enter the window, first fix the baseline to be inspected. Then preserve the first failed job; if there is a rerun that changes only the environment, record the differences alongside the original failure. Next, review the materials in build, generator, and runtime order to confirm whether they can explain the same change.

When the relationships across all three areas connect, approve only the migration scope covered by that set of materials. When a link breaks at any point, the current entry point remains the starting point for review, and the window does not vouch for the gap. Results from different baselines can each provide clues, but cannot be assembled into a complete evidence chain without corresponding relationships.

This order also constrains claims about the "merge scope". Having build-side results for one migration does not mean that neighboring migrations can share its generator or runtime conclusions; a runtime result that looks normal also does not mean that the original CI failure has lost its significance. Every approval must return to its own baseline and the scope covered by its materials.

## Addendum After Reassessment

The subsequent reassessment added two points. First, adjusting the window remains an option held in reserve, not a permanently excluded approach; proposing it again requires new evidence sufficient to connect the three types of materials. Second, the first failure and the environment rerun for CI cannot be collapsed into a single result. The former preserves the original location, while the latter explains what happened after the environment changed.

The reassessment did not rewrite unconfirmed parts as completed items. The current decision remains to retain the entry point, give no default status to window adjustments, and approve migrations according to the evidence coverage on the same baseline. The progress of the cut, continued accessibility of the entry point, or a successful environment rerun is not, on its own, sufficient to change this boundary.

For the adjacent handoff covering the CI image and Node version maintenance transition, see DOC-52. This document number is retained here only to distinguish adjacent maintenance records; the decision scope of DOC-51 remains limited to the beta branch cut, backport window, entry point selection, and the order in which evidence is arranged.

3. Record the consumer version and actual entry point.
4. Preserve the first failure output; do not overwrite it with later green results.

# CI Image and Node Switching Procedure

This maintenance does not start by replacing the CI image and then looking for the affected consumers. Consumers will continue to use the old entry point for some time, so the handoff starts with the entry point and consumption relationships: retain the old path, confirm the known consumers and versions of template-compiler, then have one consumer that can revert independently try the candidate path. Without these records, keep the page marked as in migration.

The draft starts by searching for the call names `tests/node/template-compiler-test.js` and `template-compiler`; keep this direction. They help expand the leads, but the test files themselves do not establish ownership of image maintenance, and the number of search hits cannot be used to calculate how many consumers have migrated. Record the inventory by consumption relationship: which entry point the consumer actually uses, which Node version it consumes, and whether it can independently return to the old entry point if it fails.

```text
Old entry (existing CI image / Node version)
        |
        v
Confirm template-compiler consumers and consumer versions
        |
        v
Candidate path: a single independently revertible consumer
        |
        +--> Failure: save the first output, restore the old entry
        |
        v
Review the result, then decide whether to expand the batch
```

## Pin the old path first

Do not delete the old configuration before the first trial. The handoff table must retain at least these values:

| Item | Recorded value |
| --- | --- |
| Old entry | The path through which the consumer currently obtains the existing CI image and Node version |
| Candidate path | The image / Node version combination to try in this round |
| Consumer | The specific location confirmed to consume what is being maintained in this change |
| Consumer version | The version actually used by that consumer |
| Restore action | The operation for returning from the candidate path to the old entry |
| Handoff entry point | The location where the next person continues the investigation and operation |

"New version" cannot substitute for a candidate path. Different consumersFang Ke can list the same Node version name but obtain the image from different entry points. Conversely, confirming that one location still uses the old entry does not mean the entire template-compiler scope has not migrated.

## Inventory and trial run

Search hits need to be separated. Definitions, helper assertions, and locations that actually trigger CI are not the same kind of usage. Put entries that only identify a file or call name in pending confirmation; only entries with a confirmed entry point and consumer version, along with a known restore action, may enter the trial batch. Without a version, it is impossible to determine whom the candidate path affects; without an entry point, later people cannot reproduce the same maintenance path.

For the first trial, choose one with a clear restore action, not the one that is easiest to rerun to green. Before connecting the candidate path, write down that consumer's current entry point and Node version. After execution, save the first failure output observed, including the failure node and the entry point used at the time; if there is no failure this time, record the corresponding consumer and version. A successful later rerun only shows that the later execution passed; it cannot erase the first observation.

The trial result changes only this consumer's status. Do not mark the other confirmed or pending items as complete just because this one passed. Before expanding the batch, verify that the old entry is still available, that the consumer can actually recover independently, and that the first result is in the handoff record. If any one of these is missing, stop with the current consumer.

## Recovery and batch handoff

The restore action must return the consumer to the old entry recorded before the trial, while retaining the candidate path's failure output and the consumer version. This is what allows later investigation to distinguish a change caused by the candidate image / Node version from instability that already existed in the consumer. Once the old entry is usable again after restoration, record "Candidate path was not expanded further"; do not write that all issues have been resolved. There is currently no evidence to attribute the failures of all template-compiler consumers to the same cause.

Each time a consumer is added, record its own version, actual entry point, and restore action; do not copy the previous row directly. If the entry point is confirmed but the version is still pending, or if the candidate path has been tried but the restore action has not been rechecked, retain the corresponding status and do not include it in the next batch. A consumer that cannot revert independently is not a trial candidate.

The handoff must retain the actual entry point, consumer version, first failure output, and handoff entry point. Leaving only one green link from a rerun does not tell later people which consumer it covered or where the first failure occurred. For the compatibility consultation entry point for runtime-compat, follow DOC-53; do not mix it into this round's CI image and Node version inventory.
